lesson.title: Three Resistors, One Center: The Wye Configuration
lesson.summary: A wye configuration connects three resistors from a common center node out to three separate terminals, forming a star whose terminal to terminal resistance is just a series sum.
lesson.body:
A wye configuration, also called a star, and sometimes a T configuration in two port circuit contexts, connects three resistors from a common center node out to three separate terminals. Label the terminals A, B, and C as before, and let N be the shared center node. The wye consists of resistor Ra between A and N, resistor Rb between B and N, and resistor Rc between C and N. In three phase power systems this center node is often the physical neutral point, sometimes grounded, sometimes left floating depending on the system design.

Because every branch meets at the same center node, finding the resistance between any two wye terminals is much simpler than the equivalent calculation for a delta. Measuring between terminals A and B, with terminal C left open and unconnected to anything, no current has anywhere to go through Rc: an open branch carries zero current and therefore drops zero voltage, so it is electrically invisible for that particular measurement. What remains is just Ra and Rb in series, forming a plain series circuit between A and B through the center node, exactly the simple addition rule from series circuits.

Take a balanced wye where all three branch resistors are equal: Ra = Rb = Rc = 10 ohm. The resistance between terminals A and B, with C open, is simply Ra plus Rb, or 10 ohm plus 10 ohm, which is 20 ohm.

That 20 ohm figure is not a coincidence. It is exactly the same terminal to terminal resistance found in the previous chapter for a balanced delta with all three resistors equal to 30 ohm. Two networks that look completely different internally, one a closed triangle with no center node, the other a star with a shared center, produce identical behavior at every pair of external terminals. Neither network can be told apart from the outside using resistance measurements alone. That is a striking result, and it is not a special property of these particular numbers, it holds in general between any delta and its matching wye, which is exactly what the delta wye transformation formulas, covered next, make precise and usable for arbitrary, unbalanced resistor values.

Beyond the mathematics, the wye configuration has a real practical advantage over the delta: its center node gives three phase power systems an actual physical neutral wire, which provides a return path for current when the three phases are not perfectly balanced. A delta connected system has no such point to tap, which is one reason wye connections are so common in residential and commercial power distribution, even though a delta can be electrically equivalent for balanced loads.

The wye's center node also makes internal currents far easier to reason about than a delta's do. Because Ra, Rb, and Rc all meet at the single node N, the current flowing into N from any one terminal branch has to equal the sum of the currents flowing out through the other two, a direct application of Kirchhoff's Current Law at that one node. A delta has no such shared node to apply KCL to directly, its three resistors only meet each other at the outer terminals, which is exactly why solving for internal currents in a delta usually means converting it to a wye first, doing the easier series style reasoning the wye allows, and converting back only if the delta's physical terminals are what the original problem asked about.
